steps.say: Most deep bleeds stay medical, but location changes everything. A cerebellar clot behaves nothing like a putaminal one.
steps.tx: **STICH trials** (surgery studies 1 and 2) found no general functional benefit from early open evacuation of **supratentorial ICH** (above tent bleeding), so routine craniotomy for deep hypertensive bleeds is not done and **individualised surgery** (case by case choice) rules accessible lobar clots with deterioration.

vis.alt: Coronal brain with ruptured lenticulostriate microaneurysm, parenchymal haematoma and head CT.
vis.caption: Hypertensive parenchymal haematoma from lenticulostriate rupture. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Small tubes into the clot changed the equation. Image-guided catheter evacuation helps selected deep clots.
steps.tx: **MISTIE III** (keyhole trial) showed minimally invasive catheter evacuation with **alteplase** (clot busting drug) lowers mortality without improving function, keeping the technique for trial-selected supratentorial clots of 30 mL or more rather than routine use, dosed 1 mg every 8 hours to 15 mL residue.

steps.say: Speed matters for surface clots. Getting the tube in within a day improves real function, not just survival.
steps.tx: **ENRICH** (early tube trial) showed early parafascicular minimally invasive evacuation within **24 hours** (one day) improves function for lobar bleeds, making small-tube **trans-sulcal surgery** (groove route operation) the modern option for accessible clots with mass effect, enrolling lobar clots of 30 to 80 mL operated early.

steps.say: The posterior fossa forgives nothing. Three centimetres of cerebellar blood with squashed spaces goes to theatre now.
steps.tx: **3 cm cerebellar** (operate above three centimetres) haematomas with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus from **fourth ventricular** (lower chamber) obstruction, go for **suboccipital craniectomy** (back skull removal) plus external ventricular drainage without waiting for coma, with tonsillar descent below the foramen magnum as the red-line imaging sign.

steps.say: Blood inside the ventricles blocks the plumbing. Washing it out through a drain trades mortality even when function stays flat.
steps.tx: **CLEAR III** (ventricle wash trial) found **intraventricular alteplase** (chamber clot buster) irrigation through an EVD lowers mortality but not function, so it is offered for small parenchymal clots with massive ventricular blood causing **obstructive hydrocephalus** (blocked water flow), with dosing through the drain and clamping intervals protocolised by the trial.

steps.say: A big stroke swells like a bleed. Half the middle cerebral territory gone means the bone comes off within two days.
steps.tx: **Malignant middle cerebral artery infarction** (giant stroke, **malignant MCA infarct**) with more than **50 percent** (half) territory oedema and midline shift needs **hemicraniectomy** (half skull removal) within **48 hours** (two days), which roughly triples survival and doubles survival with independence in patients below **60 years** (sixty years) per DECIMAL, DESTINY and HAMLET.

vis.alt: Coronal stroke section with infarct core and penumbra plus Circle of Willis vascular territories.
vis.caption: Infarct core, penumbra and middle cerebral artery territory. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Over sixty the calculus shifts. Surgery still saves life, but most survivors need daily help, and families must hear that first.
steps.tx: Above **60 years** (sixty years) hemicraniectomy still saves life per **DESTINY II** (elderly trial) but most survivors stay dependent, so the family discussion explicitly trades survival against likely **dependency** (daily care need) before consenting anyone, with dominant-hemisphere strokes counselled for likely aphasia even after survival.

steps.say: Cerebellar infarcts follow the same mass effect logic. Squashed fluid spaces around the midbrain trigger decompression plus drainage.
steps.tx: Decompressive surgery for **cerebellar infarct** (small-brain stroke) with brainstem compression follows the same mass-effect logic as cerebellar bleeds: effaced **quadrigeminal cisterns** (midbrain fluid spaces) or hydrocephalus trigger **suboccipital decompression** (back skull opening) plus drainage without delay, while brainstem infarcts themselves are rarely operated and managed supportively.
